Why it matters

There is no second take.

The flowers get thrown away. The cake gets eaten. The furniture gets packed down at midnight. Every other part of the day is temporary by design.

The photographs and the film are the only part you keep — and the only booking you cannot redo if it goes wrong. That's why it's worth spending an afternoon getting this one right.

Questions

The honest answers

How much does a wedding photographer cost in Australia?
Most Australian couples spend between $2,500 and $5,500 on wedding photography. Around $1,800 to $2,800 typically buys six to eight hours with a single shooter and an online gallery; $3,500 to $6,000 buys full-day coverage, a second shooter and an album; and established or in-demand photographers commonly sit above $6,000. Location matters — metropolitan Sydney and Melbourne sit at the higher end, and regional or off-peak dates lower it.
How much does an event photographer cost?
For a party, function or corporate event, expect roughly $150 to $400 an hour, usually with a two or three hour minimum. A two-hour birthday or launch commonly lands between $400 and $900; a half-day corporate event with edited images delivered quickly is more often $900 to $2,000. Same-day or next-day turnaround, multiple shooters and travel outside the metro area all add to it.
How many hours of wedding photography do I need?
Six hours covers the ceremony, portraits and the early reception. Eight hours is the most-booked option and gets you from getting ready through to the first dance. Ten hours or full-day coverage is what you need if getting ready starts early, the venues are far apart, or you want the dance floor properly covered. If you're unsure, map your running sheet first — the answer usually falls out of it.
Do I need both a photographer and a videographer?
They hold different things. Stills are what you print, frame and put on a wall — they survive being looked at a thousand times. Film holds what a photo can't: their voice during the vows, the sound of the room during the speeches, the way your grandmother laughed. Couples who book both most often say the film was the one they didn't expect to watch as much as they do. If the budget only stretches to one, most photographers will tell you to book photography first.
How far in advance should I book a wedding photographer?
Twelve months ahead is comfortable, and the photographers with the strongest portfolios are often booked twelve to eighteen months out for peak-season Saturdays — roughly October through April. For events and parties, four to eight weeks is usually enough. If your date is sooner than that, enquire anyway; availability shifts and mid-week or off-season dates open up far more choice.
Should I hire two photographers for my wedding?
A second shooter is worth it when getting ready happens in two locations, when your guest count is above about 120, or when the reception is in a dark or complex venue. The real gain is simultaneous coverage — one on the aisle and one on your partner's face during the vows, which a single photographer physically cannot do. For an intimate wedding under 80 guests in one location, one experienced photographer is usually plenty.
How long does it take to receive wedding photos?
Four to eight weeks is the industry norm for a full gallery, with a preview set of 20 to 50 images commonly delivered within a week. Films take longer — six to twelve weeks for a highlight film is typical because editing, colour grading and sound take time. Ask for the turnaround in writing before you book, and be cautious of anyone promising a full wedding gallery in a few days.
What's included in an event photography package?
Usually the shooting time, professional editing, and delivery of high-resolution images through an online gallery with a print licence. What varies — and what you should confirm — is travel, whether a second shooter is included, how many final images you receive, album or print costs, raw file access (most photographers won't hand these over), and how long the gallery stays online. Get the inclusions itemised rather than quoted as one number.
